sources.news_title: U.S. House passes govt funding stopgap to avoid shutdown
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – The U.S. House passed a short-term continuing resolution to keep government funding on cruise control past the looming Oct.1 shutdown date, sending the bill over to the Senate.
The CR would ensure federal agencies are funded until Dec. 4, buying lawmakers more time to finish passing all 12 annual appropriations bills. Currently, not a single appropriations bill has passed both chambers of Congress.
"The hard reality before us is straightforward – the fiscal year deadline is outpacing the work that remains,” House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., told lawmakers before the vote.
“Our conference refuses to let the obstruction and inaction of Senate Democrats trigger another manufactured shutdown at the end of September. That is why we are acting before a funding lapse crisis, not in response to it.”
If lawmakers do not appropriate new funds or temporarily freeze funding at current levels, the government shuts down, as has already happened twice in the 119th Congress. Yet many Democrats are indicating they are willing to take that risk, with all but six opposing the CR in the late Tuesday night House vote.
“The House Republican continuing resolution gives the Trump administration even more power over the federal budget and fails to block funding for Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation regime,” House Democratic leadership released in a joint statement explaining their opposition.
“This continuing resolution is a premature and desperate attempt by Republicans to abdicate their responsibility to govern while there are still several months left to negotiate a bipartisan agreement.”
Though the CR now heads to the Senate for approval, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., indicated that chamber leadership has its own plans.
Thune told reporters that Senate appropriations from both parties are “working…to find a path forward” on a CR to keep the government funded past the November midterm elections.
“I think it's going to be really important that we figure out a path forward to get a bipartisan agreement to fund the government, that will keep the government open and ensure that government employees are getting paid,” Thune said Tuesday night.
“That is something that I intend to bring to the floor for a vote before the August break,” he added. “And that depends a little bit on cooperation right now. It's possible that that would be something that would get punted into September.”
Thune’s bipartisan approach may be crucial to averting a third costly shutdown, since congressional Democrats have already proven they are willing to block government funding over immigration policy.
Senate Democrats triggered the longest government shutdown in history in February, a 76-day shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security, over demands that Republicans implement drastic reforms to ICE and Border Patrol.
Democrats only voted to end the shutdown when Republicans stripped immigration enforcement funding from the Homeland Security appropriations bill entirely, though Republicans later infused ICE and Border Patrol with a three-year cash advance via a budget reconciliation bill.

sources.news_title: House Passes Govt Funding Through Dec., Securing Operations for Border Enforcement
House Passes Major Bill — Lauren Boebert RUNS to Floor for CLOSE Vote
sources.text:
House Republicans have passed a blockbuster bill this week, leaving Democrats powerless to stop it from making its way to President Donald Trump’s desk for signature.
The U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday passed H.R. 9770, a continuing resolution that will fund the full federal government through December 4, 2026.
The measure passed by a vote of 220-205.
Republicans provided overwhelming support with 213 yes votes against just one no, while six Democrats joined in support and one Independent voted yes.
Four Republicans and two Democrats did not vote.
The single Republican “no” vote came from a fiscal conservative who has consistently opposed short-term funding extensions on principle.
The vote came under the gavel of Rep. Kat Cammack (R-FL) serving as Speaker Pro Tempore.
Passage clears a key hurdle to prevent a government funding lapse that could disrupt operations across federal agencies.
H.R. 9770 is a clean continuing resolution that extends current funding levels and authorities for federal programs and agencies through December 4.
It maintains operations at the rates and conditions set in prior appropriations, avoiding the need for a full-year spending package at this time while Congress continues its work on longer-term measures.
The bill ensures continuity for critical functions, including national security, law enforcement, veterans’ services, and infrastructure.
By extending funding into early December, it provides stability through the fall and into the holiday period, avoiding the uncertainty of a potential shutdown.
The measure carries particular significance for border security and immigration enforcement.
It prevents Democrats from leveraging a funding gap to restrict resources for the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a tactic observers note was attempted in prior cycles.
With stable funding in place, DHS can proceed without interruption in its core missions, including the ramp-up of interior enforcement and deportations under the Trump administration’s priorities.
Conservatives have long argued that repeated Democratic threats to withhold or condition DHS funding amount to holding border security hostage for unrelated policy demands.
Tuesday’s vote removes that leverage in the near term and keeps resources flowing to agents and officers tasked with enforcing immigration law.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) signaled he will move the measure through the upper chamber expeditiously.
With Republican control of the Senate, Thune is expected to bring H.R. 9770 to the floor quickly, likely with limited debate, and send it to President Trump’s desk for signature in short order.
Rep. Boebert running up the stairs to make it to votes pic.twitter.com/k7Lk3Hkag7
— Acyn (@Acyn) July 22, 2026
The rapid timeline reflects GOP leadership’s determination to deliver stable funding and avoid any disruption to ongoing enforcement operations.
This action aligns with the broader Republican strategy of maintaining government functions while advancing America First priorities.
By securing funding without major concessions, House Republicans have protected the operational capacity of agencies responsible for border control and interior enforcement at a time when the administration is accelerating deportations of individuals unlawfully present in the United States.
The handful of Democrats who crossed the aisle represent moderates or members from competitive districts who recognized the practical need to keep essential services running.
The passage of H.R. 9770 underscores a key difference in governing philosophy.
Republicans have prioritized keeping essential services running for the American people while ensuring that procedural brinkmanship does not deprive border enforcement agencies of resources.
With the bill headed to the Senate under Thune’s leadership, the focus now shifts to swift final approval and continued progress on full-year appropriations that further strengthen national security and fiscal discipline.
Stable funding through December allows ICE and DHS to operate at full capacity, supporting the administration’s commitment to large-scale removals and restoring order to the immigration system.
This article may contain commentary which reflects the author's opinion.

sources.news_title: House Passes CR Through Dec. 4, But Senate GOP Wants a Different Bill
sources.text:
The House on Tuesday passed a continuing resolution extending government funding at current levels through Dec. 4, pushing the shutdown deadline past the November midterms in a 220-205 vote, even as Congress has yet to pass a single one of its 12 annual appropriations bills through both chambers.
WHAT HAPPENED
The measure passed largely along party lines, with six Democrats — Reps. Kathy Castor of Florida, Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, Don Davis of North Carolina, Jared Golden of Maine and Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico — breaking with party leadership to vote yes, while Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky was the only Republican to vote no. House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole had described the measure as "clean and straightforward," free of "poison pills," extending current funding levels for programs including SNAP, WIC, TANF, the National Flood Insurance Program, wildfire suppression, the disaster relief fund and small business support. The House had already advanced all 12 fiscal year 2027 appropriations bills through committee and passed three full-year measures on the floor, but the Senate has yet to pass any of its versions.
House Democratic leadership argued the bill "fails to block" funding for border enforcement operations, according to lawmakers who cited it as their reason for opposing the measure; House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro had said before the vote that Democrats wanted, "at a minimum," funding guarantees related to Border Patrol operations before backing it. Government funding is currently set to run out Sept. 30. Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans "took the responsible step of passing a clean, short-term continuing resolution to fund our government through the November elections," criticizing Democrats for opposing it.
The bill now heads to the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has said he is preparing an alternative stopgap measure rather than immediately taking up the House-passed version, potentially setting up a standoff between the chambers before senators leave for a monthlong August recess. The current funding fight comes after Democrats blocked government funding measures for a record 43 days last year in a dispute over expiring health care tax credits, and twice more this year over immigration enforcement policy following the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis.
WHY IT MATTERS
Passage of the measure through the House, even by a narrow and largely party-line margin, demonstrates Speaker Johnson can still hold his slim majority together on a high-stakes funding vote, but the emerging standoff with Thune's Senate signals the fight is far from resolved. Extending funding through Dec. 4 would keep federal agencies open past Election Day, removing a shutdown threat from the immediate pre-midterm political calendar even as it defers the underlying appropriations fight to the lame-duck period after voters go to the polls. Democrats' focus on Border Patrol funding assurances, rather than broader spending levels, signals that immigration enforcement remains the central sticking point bleeding into unrelated budget negotiations, a dynamic that has repeatedly triggered shutdowns over the past year. That none of the 12 annual appropriations bills has passed both chambers this far into the fiscal year underscores how thoroughly the regular budget process has broken down, with stopgap measures increasingly serving as the default mechanism for keeping the government funded.
WHAT'S NEXT
The bill's fate now depends on the Senate, where Thune's preference for crafting an alternative CR rather than adopting the House version could delay resolution and create renewed uncertainty ahead of the Oct. 1 deadline. Whether Thune's approach draws enough bipartisan support to pass, or whether it triggers a standoff with the House similar to past funding fights, will determine if Congress can avoid a shutdown before the August recess concludes. Continued disagreement over Border Patrol and other immigration-related funding is likely to remain the central flashpoint as negotiations continue toward whatever new deadline emerges from the Senate's version.

sources.news_title: House passes bill to fund the government through midterm elections
House Advances Stopgap Funding Bill as Senate Clash Looms - Internewscast Journal
House passes temporary government funding bill months early
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House moved Tuesday to head-off a potential government shutdown before this fall’s critical midterm elections by passing a bill to fund the federal government through Dec. 4.
The deadline for action is more than two months away, but House GOP leaders are not leaving to chance another possible shutdown souring the mood of voters shortly before they go to the polls. House Speaker Mike Johnson dared Democrats to vote against the bill, and if they did, “then they alone are going to own the chaos that ensues if the government shuts down after September 30.”
The House passed the measure by a mostly party-line vote of 220-205.
It’s highly unusual for Congress to pass a stopgap funding bill months before the end of the fiscal year. Lawmakers normally act just days or even hours before the deadline. But once lawmakers leave town this week, the House is scheduled to be in session for only 16 more days before the funding deadline.
GOP leadership is laying the groundwork to spend most of that time on another priority: a long-shot, party-line bill that spends $95 billion to boost defense, aid farmers and get portions of President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill passed into law.
“I think it’s kind of smart to go ahead and take the potential chaos of a shutdown off the table because the amount of damage that does to the American citizens,” said Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga. He said he believed a shutdown “probably works to the advantage of Democrats politically,” and he blamed the press for such a scenario.
Democrats overwhelmingly opposed the stopgap measure, which would generally fund agencies at current spending levels.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said the legislation was dropped on Democrats on Friday without any bipartisan negotiations. She said that, among other priorities, Democrats would have pushed for provisions to reverse a proposed federal rule that could allow agency heads to block or terminate grants they claim don’t match the president’s priorities.
She said that instead of a bipartisan agreement, “we are scrambling to jam through a one-sided stopgap measure two days before everyone leaves for the August recess.”
Republicans said work on the dozen annual spending bills would continue in the months ahead, but that funding the government through Dec. 4 could help lawmakers avoid a repeat of the past year when the country experienced the longest federal shutdown in history followed by the longest partial shutdown in history.
“We’ve seen that happen twice in this Congress already,” said Rep. Tom Cole, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. “I’m not willing to risk a third time if we can avoid that.”
Some of the more conservative Republican lawmakers were fine with the bill to extend funding to Dec. 4, known as a continuing resolution.
In this environment, that’s “the best way to spend the least amount of money,” said Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo. “You keep spending levels static for at least a period of time.”
It’s unclear if the Senate will go along with the bill. Spending bills require support from 60 senators to advance to a final vote, so some Democrats would need to support it. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters that Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins was working with Democrats on the committee to “find a path forward.”

The so-called continuing resolution cleared the lower chamber in a 2020-205 vote.

“They apparently believe a painful government shutdown would help them politically. We hope they will come to their senses before the government shuts down, but if they don’t, then Democrats alone will own the chaos that results.”

The bill “does not continue that agreement,” DeLauro fumed, according to CBS News, “giving the Trump administration permission to use billions provided by this bill to fund Border Patrol without any substantial reforms to how that agency operates.”
“It’s a clear line in the sand that Democrats have drawn for months,” she added.

sources.news_title: Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct. 1 deadline
sources.text:
Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct. 1 deadline
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — The U.S. House approved a stopgap spending bill Tuesday that would keep the government up and running through the fall, sending it to the Senate, where lawmakers expect to rework the measure.
Congress must pass a government funding bill before the new fiscal year starts on Oct. 1 in order to avoid a shutdown just weeks before the November midterm elections.
The 220-205 mostly party-line vote represents House Republicans’ opening salvo in negotiations, though without Democratic support it won’t be able to advance in the Senate.
House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said during floor debate that GOP leaders hope passing the stopgap spending bill months before the start of the next fiscal year will avoid another shutdown.
“For anyone questioning this legislation, the facts are simple — it extends the government funding deadline to Dec. 4, denying any party the opportunity to manufacture leverage before elections,” Cole said. “It contains no poison pills or partisan riders. It prevents harmful disruptions to our national security and the vital programs our constituents rely on.”
Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the committee, opposed the stopgap, saying it would “allow Homeland Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin to transfer billions of dollars to the Border Patrol.”
Republicans, she said, “refused” to change that aspect of the bill after Democrats “shared language to fix it.”
“We cannot in good conscience allow billions of dollars to flow to these agencies without major reforms to keep our constituents safe from further violence,” DeLauro said.
Democrats don’t want a government shutdown but also don’t want “to rush” the process and omit the list of anomalies just sent up by the White House, she said.
Those tweaks to funding levels are commonly added to stopgap spending bills but weren’t included in House Republicans’ measure because it was written before the White House sent a list of requested anomalies to lawmakers Monday.
“There are over 50 programs listed by the agencies to take some action so that they can be protected during a continuing resolution,” DeLauro said, using the technical term for a short-term funding bill.
The changes would support wildfire suppression activities, housing assistance for tens of thousands and programs that help people in rural communities afford their utilities.
“Rushing this bill to the floor haphazardly without carefully considering the various needs that must be met is no way to govern,” DeLauro said. “And it is irresponsible.”
Senate anticipates changes
Senate Appropriations Committee Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, said earlier in the day that she was working with the committee’s top Democrat, Washington Sen. Patty Murray, to draft a continuing resolution of their own.
“It appears that there is good faith on the Democratic side to try to pass the CR and avoid a government shutdown, which is always a disaster,” Collins said.
Murray said the House’s stopgap spending bill has “problems” that will need to be fixed in order to move through the Senate.
“We just got the anomalies last night and both of us are trying to figure out the best way to get it put together,” Murray said.
Appropriations status
Lawmakers must lean on a stopgap spending bill because they will, once again, fail to complete work on the dozen annual government funding bills before the deadline.
The House has passed three of its spending bills. The Senate hasn’t passed any, in part, because the committee hasn’t released a single bill. The two chambers will need to begin negotiations at some point to settle on a total spending level for the 12 bills and how that roughly $1.9 trillion will be broken down among thousands of federal agencies and programs.
That means the earliest the full-year government spending bills would become law is during the lame-duck session that is set to last for about five weeks between the election and the start of the new Congress in January.
Lawmakers could also pass a series of stopgap funding bills instead of completing negotiations on the full-year appropriations bills.

sources.news_title: House narrowly passes short-term funding bill to avert government shutdown
sources.text:
House narrowly passes short-term funding bill to avert government shutdown
The vote sends the stopgap, known as a continuing resolution, to the Senate.
WASHINGTON - The Republican-controlled U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday passed a short-term measure to avert a possible government shutdown ahead of the November midterm elections by funding federal agencies through December 4.
The vote sends the stopgap, known as a continuing resolution, to the Senate, where Republican leaders are exploring their own short-term funding bill in negotiations with Democrats.
The resolution authorizing government spending narrowly passed by a vote of 220-205.
Without action by Congress, funding for most federal agency programs will expire at midnight on September 30, the end of the current fiscal year.
The shutdown threat is the latest over the past several years. In April, Congress finally ended a historic Department of Homeland Security shutdown, resolving the longest crisis of its kind in American history.
The April vote resolved a political showdown that plagued Capitol Hill and the country for about 75 days. The ordeal, which exposed fierce acrimony between House and Senate Republicans, left thousands of workers without pay, upended air travel and jeopardized Americans' safety.
The impasse was prompted by congressional Democrats' demands for immigration enforcement reforms after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good. Yet the big changes they wanted, such as a ban on masks for officers and judicial warrant requirements for immigration raids, never materialized.

"We've seen that happen twice in this Congress already," said Rep. Tom Cole, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. "I'm not willing to risk a third time if we can avoid that."
Some of the more conservative Republican lawmakers were fine with the bill to extend funding to Dec. 4, known as a continuing resolution.
In this environment, that's "the best way to spend the least amount of money," said Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo. "You keep spending levels static for at least a period of time."
It's unclear if the Senate will go along with the bill. Spending bills require support from 60 senators to advance to a final vote, so some Democrats would need to support it. sources.news_title: Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct.1 deadline
sources.text:
Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct.1 deadline
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — The U.S. House approved a stopgap spending bill Tuesday that would keep the government up and running through the fall, sending it to the Senate, where lawmakers expect to rework the measure.
Congress must pass a government funding bill before the new fiscal year starts on Oct. 1 in order to avoid a shutdown just weeks before the November midterm elections.
The 220-205 mostly party-line vote represents House Republicans’ opening salvo in negotiations, though without Democratic support it won’t be able to advance in the Senate.
House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said during floor debate that GOP leaders hope passing the stopgap spending bill months before the start of the next fiscal year will avoid another shutdown.
“For anyone questioning this legislation, the facts are simple — it extends the government funding deadline to Dec. 4, denying any party the opportunity to manufacture leverage before elections,” Cole said. “It contains no poison pills or partisan riders. It prevents harmful disruptions to our national security and the vital programs our constituents rely on.”
Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the committee, opposed the stopgap, saying it would “allow Homeland Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin to transfer billions of dollars to the Border Patrol.”
Republicans, she said, “refused” to change that aspect of the bill after Democrats “shared language to fix it.”
“We cannot in good conscience allow billions of dollars to flow to these agencies without major reforms to keep our constituents safe from further violence,” DeLauro said.
Democrats don’t want a government shutdown but also don’t want “to rush” the process and omit the list of anomalies just sent up by the White House, she said.
Those tweaks to funding levels are commonly added to stopgap spending bills but weren’t included in House Republicans’ measure because it was written before the White House sent a list of requested anomalies to lawmakers Monday.
“There are over 50 programs listed by the agencies to take some action so that they can be protected during a continuing resolution,” DeLauro said, using the technical term for a short-term funding bill.
The changes would support wildfire suppression activities, housing assistance for tens of thousands and programs that help people in rural communities afford their utilities.
“Rushing this bill to the floor haphazardly without carefully considering the various needs that must be met is no way to govern,” DeLauro said. “And it is irresponsible.”
Senate anticipates changes
Senate Appropriations Committee Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, said earlier in the day that she was working with the committee’s top Democrat, Washington Sen. Patty Murray, to draft a continuing resolution of their own.
“It appears that there is good faith on the Democratic side to try to pass the CR and avoid a government shutdown, which is always a disaster,” Collins said.
Murray said the House’s stopgap spending bill has “problems” that will need to be fixed in order to move through the Senate.
“We just got the anomalies last night and both of us are trying to figure out the best way to get it put together,” Murray said.
Appropriations status
Lawmakers must lean on a stopgap spending bill because they will, once again, fail to complete work on the dozen annual government funding bills before the deadline.
The House has passed three of its spending bills. The Senate hasn’t passed any, in part, because the committee hasn’t released a single bill. The two chambers will need to begin negotiations at some point to settle on a total spending level for the 12 bills and how that roughly $1.9 trillion will be broken down among thousands of federal agencies and programs.
That means the earliest the full-year government spending bills would become law is during the lame-duck session that is set to last for about five weeks between the election and the start of the new Congress in January.
Lawmakers could also pass a series of stopgap funding bills instead of completing negotiations on the full-year appropriations bills.

sources.text:
House passes short-term bill to punt government funding fight past midterm elections
Washington — The House on Tuesday approved a short-term extension to fund the government until Dec. 4, hoping to punt the annual funding fight past the November midterm elections.
The funding patch, known as a continuing resolution, passed in a 220 to 205 vote. Six Democrats voted with all but one Republican in favor.
"The CR is as clean as they come. There are no poison pills. There's no maneuvers. There's nothing other than a simple extension of current funding levels," House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said Tuesday.
Its passage comes days before the House is set to leave Washington for its five-week August recess. The measure now heads to the Senate, which is scheduled to be in town through the first week of August.
Government funding runs out on Sept. 30, leaving lawmakers limited time to avoid a shutdown before they head into the final stretch of campaign season.
"We want to take away the possibility of a shutdown between now and the election," House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, an Oklahoma Republican, said Monday. "We've seen that happen twice in this Congress already, generated by the Senate, and I'm not willing to risk a third time if we can avoid that."
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday that he will put a short-term spending bill on the floor before the upper chamber goes on recess.
"That is something that I intend to bring to the floor for a vote before the August break," the South Dakota Republican said.
Thune also indicated that he could use the House's budget resolution, which the lower chamber hopes to pass later this week, as a vehicle to fund the government through November. That resolution would kickstart the reconciliation process, which allows Senate Republicans to pass funding bills with a simple majority and no Democratic votes.
"I hope that's not necessary," he said. "We've had conversations, productive conversations, on both sides of the aisle on a funding resolution that would carry us past the November election."
Since April, the House Appropriations Committee has advanced all 12 annual appropriations bills that fund the federal government. Three have been approved by the full House. The process, however, has broken down in the Senate, where none of the funding measures have made it out of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
House Republicans' continuing resolution extends funding at current levels and excludes any controversial add-ons — something Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, acknowledged Monday.
But DeLauro said she would not support the measure because it fails to carry over a provision that zeroed out funding for Border Patrol, which she argued would allow the Trump administration to move funds allotted to the rest of Customs and Border Protection to the agency. In April, Congress passed a bill to fund most of the Department of Homeland Security — with the exception of immigration enforcement agencies — that ended the lengthiest government shutdown in U.S. history.
"Chairman Cole's bill does not continue that agreement, giving the Trump administration permission to use billions provided by this bill to fund Border Patrol without any substantial reforms to how that agency operates," DeLauro said. "It's a clear line in the sand that Democrats have drawn for months."
In a statement ahead of the vote, House Democratic leaders called the measure "a premature and desperate attempt by Republicans to abdicate their responsibility to govern while there are still several months left to negotiate a bipartisan agreement."
"The House Republican continuing resolution gives the Trump administration even more power over the federal budget and fails to block funding for Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine," Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Minority Whip Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California said.

House GOP votes to punt government shutdown battle to after November midterms
The House of Representatives voted on Tuesday night to punt the threat of another government shutdown until after the November midterm elections.
House lawmakers passed a bill to extend the current fiscal year’s funding levels until Dec. 4 via a measure called a continuing resolution (CR). It would extend several weeks into fiscal year (FY) 2027, which begins on Oct. 1.

SENATE WEIGHS NEW, PAINFUL LEVERAGE TACTIC AS FEARS OF ANOTHER GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN GROW

“As the marxists and communists battle it out for control of the Democrat party, House Republicans are proving yet again that we are the party that governs and works for the American people. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are the party of commonsense. The other side — led by Commie Mamdani — is the party of chaos and destruction. A majority of Democrats just voted for another damning Schumer Shutdown,” he said in reference to New York City’s self-proclaimed Democratic Socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
The current fiscal year saw the longest government shutdown in history, lasting from Oct. 1, 2025 until Nov. 12, 2025, as Senate Democrats blockaded GOP-led funding priorities for weeks in protest of spending cuts to federal healthcare programs.
And Republicans are warning that Democrats would almost certainly cause another government shutdown right before the election if the fight is not punted until after the early November midterms.
“Unfortunately, given that Democrats have already forced the two longest government shutdowns in American history in this Congress, one of them for 78 days, they’ve already demonstrated they don’t care what kind of pain they inflict on the American people,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “They’ve shown there’s nothing they’d love more than a government shutdown as tens of millions of Americans head to the polls in November.”
House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., told reporters Tuesday that he would vote against the bill along with the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, the panel tasked with overseeing yearly federal spending.
“I think that there are some drafting errors within the CR that give Customs and Border Patrol flexibility to move money around. The administration said that all of that was funded within reconciliation 2.0. and I think they’re creating other opportunities to transfer funds,” Aguilar said.
But even with the House’s victory, it’s not clear that the fight will be over before September.
HOUSE GOP PUSHES BACK ON SENATE’S ‘SKINNY’ PLAN TO END RECORD-BREAKING DHS SHUTDOWN
The GOP-led Senate is working on its own course on funding extension, with sources familiar with the process telling Fox News Digital that appropriators were crafting their own CR. They believe the House’s product lacked key extensions to certain programs that are expected to run out of funding come the Sept. 30 deadline.
Those programs, known as anomalies, were shipped to the Senate from the White House on Monday.
Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Fox News Digital that Republicans and Democrats, for the time being, were working together to thwart a shutdown.
He hoped to get the CR onto the floor as soon as this week, given that the House is set to leave Washington, D.C., by the end of the week for a long August recess.
“Look, we appreciate the House moving forward with theirs. It’s, you know, very clean,” Hoeven said. “There are just a few issues that we think need to be the rest. Because, obviously, we need to get Democrats on board with us, right now, they’re working with us.”
The move has the full blessing of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.
“I think it’s going to be really important that we figure out a path forward to get a bipartisan agreement to fund the government that will keep government open and ensure that government employees are getting paid,” Thune said. “And that is something that I intend to bring to the floor for a vote before the August break.

sources.news_title: House passes stopgap bill to fund government as Senate eyes alternative
Funding extension passes House, heads for Senate rewrite
sources.text:
Funding extension passes House, heads for Senate rewrite
Stopgap could be poised for ping-ponging between chambers
The House passed a short-term funding patch Tuesday night that is designed to head off a partial government shutdown this fall.
The continuing resolution passed on a mostly party-line vote of 220-205, with only one Republican — Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie — joining most Democrats in opposition. Six Democrats broke with their party to support the measure: Reps. Kathy Castor of Florida, Henry Cuellar of Texas, Don Davis of North Carolina, Jared Golden of Maine, Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, and Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico.
The stopgap measure would extend current funding through Dec. 4, providing about an extra two months to complete full appropriations bills for the fiscal year that begins Oct. 1.
But the bill that emerged from the House is unlikely to be the final version. Senate Republicans have complained that it lacks many of the “anomalies,” or deviations from current spending, sought by the Trump administration to address what it sees as critical priorities, including military funding.
That concern could trigger a game of ping-pong between the two chambers before a final continuing resolution becomes law.
“I think the House will send us something, and then hopefully we’ll be able to modify it so that we can get Democrat votes on it,” Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said Tuesday. “And if we can get Democrat votes on it, send it back to the House as the best we can do.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said Tuesday that lawmakers from both sides of the aisle are working to reach an agreement on a stopgap bill that runs past the midterm elections. Thune also said he intends to bring a bill to the floor “before the August break.”
However, the House is scheduled to leave town Thursday for its August recess, while the Senate is scheduled to remain in session for an additional two weeks. The disparate legislative calendars raise the possibility that a final stopgap bill may not be ironed out until both chambers return in September.
But House leadership charged ahead with its own slimmer CR, which was drafted and released before the White House had submitted its anomaly requests. GOP leaders won a modest victory earlier Tuesday when the House adopted a rule that was needed to take up the stopgap bill, on a 214-211 vote.
Conservatives in the House say the strategy to vote on a stopgap before the coming August recess helps remove the threat of a government shutdown in the fall sooner. But some also hope the move will put pressure on Democrats ahead of the November elections.
“We also want to put a little pressure on the Senate,” House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said Tuesday, while blaming Democrats for stalled appropriations bills in the Senate. Cole said part of the hope is to “create some momentum” as appropriators look to strike what is poised to be their last major funding deal before the midterm elections.
Democratic pushback
Prominent Democrats criticized the funding extension in recent days, noting the legislation was crafted without bipartisan input and released before members could receive a list of requested anomalies from the White House. And House Democratic leaders announced their opposition to the measure Tuesday evening.
“This continuing resolution is a premature and desperate attempt by Republicans to abdicate their responsibility to govern while there are still several months left to negotiate a bipartisan agreement,” said Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and Conference Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., in a joint statement. “We will be voting No.”
In a document produced by House Democratic appropriators, the party raised concerns over whether the stopgap would provide sufficient funding for various programs through early December and said the recent list from the White House indicated “potentially serious issues left unaddressed by the Republican funding bill.”
That includes, Democrats said, “funding shortfalls for public housing agencies to maintain housing assistance,” “cuts to wildland fire suppression operations” and “USDA programs to help address utility costs in rural communities.”
House Democrats also sounded an alarm about a provision they say is missing from the bill that would prevent the Trump administration from being able to transfer additional funding to the Border Patrol. They cited language in the fiscal 2026 Homeland Security funding law that zeroes out such funding, and accused Republicans of refusing to include the prohibition in the latest stopgap.
GOP appropriators have largely pushed back on those arguments. Cole argued Tuesday that the bill “doesn’t undo anything,” while also raising the point that language explicitly blocking such funding could jeopardize GOP support.
Thune’s threat
Thune told reporters Tuesday that bipartisan talks are underway to find a path forward on funding agencies past September, but he also warned that Republicans could turn to reconciliation to fund the government if those discussions fall apart.
Thune said the Senate would hold up the budget resolution being considered in the House if it gets adopted this week, adding: “It’s a possibility that if necessary, we could pull that budget resolution passed by the House and use it to fund government.”
The budget resolution would lay the groundwork for a reconciliation package providing up to $95 billion for defense spending, farm aid and voting restrictions along the lines of the so-called SAVE America Act. But Thune appeared to suggest using that resolution to fund regular appropriations for federal agencies if the two parties reached an impasse.
“I hope that’s not necessary,” he said. “As I said, we’ve had conversations, productive conversations, on both sides of the aisle on a funding resolution that would carry us past the November election.”
But Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, an appropriator who has bristled at the use of the partisan reconciliation process to provide regular appropriations, pushed back on Thune’s reconciliation threat Tuesday night.
“You know how I feel about this,” Murkowski said. “Yeah, I don’t like the idea.”

sources.text:
The House of Representatives voted 220-205 on Tuesday to extend funding for the government at existing levels through Dec. 4.
Six Democrats joined with Republicans to advance the bill. The government is currently set to run out of money at the end of September, just before the midterm elections.
House Republican hard-liners have lately been holding up legislation in a so far fruitless effort to pressure their Senate colleagues into passing President Trump's election overhaul bill, the SAVE America Act. The legislation would require voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote and photo ID when casting a ballot. After some speculation the government funding bill could be caught up in that fight, the lawmakers let it proceed without incident.
Democratic leaders opposed the funding extension, writing in a statement that the bill "fails to block funding for Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine."
"Their my-way-or-the-highway approach has consistently failed to address the high cost of living or meet the needs of the American people," said Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif.
Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., criticized Democrats ahead of the vote for their opposition to the funding plan.
"They do this to try to score political points. I think they're making the wrong calculation here," Johnson said.
The bill now heads to the Senate, where it will require Democratic support to clear the 60-vote threshold required to pass most legislation through the chamber.
The funding effort comes after two record-setting government shutdowns during this Congress. Democrats forced a 45-day total government shutdown last year in a failed attempt to force congressional Republicans to extend federal healthcare subsidies. That shutdown was, at the time, the longest in U.S. history.
A 76-day Department of Homeland Security shutdown followed at the beginning of this year after federal immigration enforcement personnel killed two American citizens in Minnesota. Democrats refused to support funding for the agency unless Republicans backed reforms, including restrictions on face coverings and the deployment of body cameras for immigration enforcement officers. Ultimately, Republicans used a parliamentary procedure known as reconciliation to fund the agency on a party-line vote for the rest of President Trump's time in office.
The bill's path through the Senate is uncertain. Speaking with reporters at the Capitol on Tuesday, Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he would put a government funding plan to a vote before senators leave Washington for the August recess.
If Republicans are unable to reach a deal with Democrats to extend government funding, Thune said he would consider turning back to the reconciliation process to pass the bill on a strictly party-line basis.
"I hope that's not necessary," he said.

House passes temporary government funding bill months early to avoid election season shutdown
House passes temporary government funding bill months early to avoid election season shutdown
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House moved Tuesday to head-off a potential government shutdown before this fall’s critical midterm elections by passing a bill to fund the federal government through Dec. 4.
The deadline for action is more than two months away, but House GOP leaders are not leaving to chance another possible shutdown souring the mood of voters shortly before they go to the polls. House Speaker Mike Johnson dared Democrats to vote against the bill, and if they did, “then they alone are going to own the chaos that ensues if the government shuts down after September 30.”
The House passed the measure by a mostly party-line vote of 220-205.
It’s highly unusual for Congress to pass a stopgap funding bill months before the end of the fiscal year. Lawmakers normally act just days or even hours before the deadline. But once lawmakers leave town this week, the House is scheduled to be in session for only 16 more days before the funding deadline.
GOP leadership is laying the groundwork to spend most of that time on another priority: a long-shot, party-line bill that spends $95 billion to boost defense, aid farmers and get portions of President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill passed into law.
“I think it’s kind of smart to go ahead and take the potential chaos of a shutdown off the table because the amount of damage that does to the American citizens,” said Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga. He said he believed a shutdown “probably works to the advantage of Democrats politically,” and he blamed the press for such a scenario.
Democrats overwhelmingly opposed the stopgap measure, which would generally fund agencies at current spending levels.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said the legislation was dropped on Democrats on Friday without any bipartisan negotiations. She said that, among other priorities, Democrats would have pushed for provisions to reverse a proposed federal rule that could allow agency heads to block or terminate grants they claim don’t match the president’s priorities.
She said that instead of a bipartisan agreement, “we are scrambling to jam through a one-sided stopgap measure two days before everyone leaves for the August recess.”
Republicans said work on the dozen annual spending bills would continue in the months ahead, but that funding the government through Dec. 4 could help lawmakers avoid a repeat of the past year when the country experienced the longest federal shutdown in history followed by the longest partial shutdown in history.
“We’ve seen that happen twice in this Congress already,” said Rep. Tom Cole, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. “I’m not willing to risk a third time if we can avoid that.”
Some of the more conservative Republican lawmakers were fine with the bill to extend funding to Dec. 4, known as a continuing resolution.
In this environment, that’s “the best way to spend the least amount of money,” said Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo. “You keep spending levels static for at least a period of time.”
It’s unclear if the Senate will go along with the bill. Spending bills require support from 60 senators to advance to a final vote, so some Democrats would need to support it. sources.news_title: Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct. 1 deadline - Now Georgia
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. House approved a stopgap spending bill Tuesday that would keep the government up and running through the fall, sending it to the Senate, where lawmakers expect to rework the measure.
Congress must pass a government funding bill before the new fiscal year starts on Oct. 1 in order to avoid a shutdown just weeks before the November midterm elections.
The 220-205 mostly party-line vote represents House Republicans’ opening salvo in negotiations, though without Democratic support it won’t be able to advance in the Senate.
House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said during floor debate that GOP leaders hope passing the stopgap spending bill months before the start of the next fiscal year will avoid another shutdown.
“For anyone questioning this legislation, the facts are simple — it extends the government funding deadline to Dec. 4, denying any party the opportunity to manufacture leverage before elections,” Cole said. “It contains no poison pills or partisan riders. It prevents harmful disruptions to our national security and the vital programs our constituents rely on.”
Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the committee, opposed the stopgap, saying it would “allow Homeland Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin to transfer billions of dollars to the Border Patrol.”
Republicans, she said, “refused” to change that aspect of the bill after Democrats “shared language to fix it.”
“We cannot in good conscience allow billions of dollars to flow to these agencies without major reforms to keep our constituents safe from further violence,” DeLauro said.
Democrats don’t want a government shutdown but also don’t want “to rush” the process and omit the list of anomalies just sent up by the White House, she said.
Those tweaks to funding levels are commonly added to stopgap spending bills but weren’t included in House Republicans’ measure because it was written before the White House sent a list of requested anomalies to lawmakers Monday.
“There are over 50 programs listed by the agencies to take some action so that they can be protected during a continuing resolution,” DeLauro said, using the technical term for a short-term funding bill.
The changes would support wildfire suppression activities, housing assistance for tens of thousands and programs that help people in rural communities afford their utilities.
“Rushing this bill to the floor haphazardly without carefully considering the various needs that must be met is no way to govern,” DeLauro said. “And it is irresponsible.”
Senate anticipates changes
Senate Appropriations Committee Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, said earlier in the day that she was working with the committee’s top Democrat, Washington Sen. Patty Murray, to draft a continuing resolution of their own.
“It appears that there is good faith on the Democratic side to try to pass the CR and avoid a government shutdown, which is always a disaster,” Collins said.
Murray said the House’s stopgap spending bill has “problems” that will need to be fixed in order to move through the Senate.
“We just got the anomalies last night and both of us are trying to figure out the best way to get it put together,” Murray said.
Appropriations status
Lawmakers must lean on a stopgap spending bill because they will, once again, fail to complete work on the dozen annual government funding bills before the deadline.
The House has passed three of its spending bills. The Senate hasn’t passed any, in part, because the committee hasn’t released a single bill. The two chambers will need to begin negotiations at some point to settle on a total spending level for the 12 bills and how that roughly $1.9 trillion will be broken down among thousands of federal agencies and programs.
That means the earliest the full-year government spending bills would become law is during the lame-duck session that is set to last for about five weeks between the election and the start of the new Congress in January.
Lawmakers could also pass a series of stopgap funding bills instead of completing negotiations on the full-year appropriations bills.
